CLAUDE.md

Source: CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

What this is

zuarrow moves columns between R and the Apache Arrow columnar format: the C Data Interface in memory and the IPC stream and file formats on disk. It converts every Arrow type in the 1.x format to an R vector and back, reads and writes both IPC framings with LZ4 and zstd bodies, and keeps a registry that says which R class is the exact form of which Arrow type. The rule behind every conversion is exact or error: a value crosses without change or the call raises zuarrow_lossy_error naming the column and the exact target. The default is never warn or allow.

The one hard dependency is zukomp (Imports and LinkingTo), which supplies the IPC codecs. nanoarrow and arrow are Suggests only, used as test oracles. The package is not a query engine, not Parquet, not a table object model, not transport (Flight, ADBC, PyCapsule) and not a replacement for nanoarrow: its handles are nanoarrow’s handles, so a session with both loaded passes objects between them without conversion.

The specification is .agents/design.md, adopted from RFC 0041 in pedrobtz/packages. It outranks this file: CLAUDE.md orients, the design decides. Its §13 decisions are all marked (C), the maintainer’s to overturn, and its §15 open questions are still open.

Current state

Scaffolded 2026-10-21 with create-pkg.sh; no functionality yet. DESCRIPTION still carries the scaffold’s placeholder title, description and author, src/zuarrow.c holds only the R headers, and the test suite is the placeholder test. The roadmap in .agents/roadmap.md is the stub pkg-roadmap fills; it takes the package to v0.1.0.

Stage tracking

Progress toward the next version is tracked as GitHub sub-issues, so the parent issue shows a progress bar such as “6 of 7”.

  • One parent issue per target version, titled with the bare version, for example v0.1.0. v0.1.0 issue: created by pkg-roadmap.
  • One sub-issue per roadmap stage, titled as the roadmap titles it, for example Stage 3 — R interface, and linking to that section. The number of stages is whatever the roadmap has; there is no fixed scale.
  • Every tracking issue carries the stage label, so it can be told apart from bug and feature issues and left out of open-issue counts.
  • Close a stage by merging its pull request. Put Closes #<n> in the body of the stage’s pull request. Never close a stage whose exit criteria are not met; record a deviation in the roadmap first.
  • The roadmap stays authoritative. The issues record which stages are done, not what a stage requires. Adding, removing or renaming a stage means editing the roadmap and the sub-issues in the same change.
  • Each stage has a CI tier, quick or full. The roadmap sets it, and quick is the default. See Continuous integration for what each means. The second-to-last stage, Full CI, runs the full set and fixes what it finds before v0.1.0 readiness.
  • Close the parent issue when CRAN accepts the version and it is tagged. Opening a parent issue implies at least one stage sub-issue; a parent with no sub-issues shows no progress on the board.

Versioning

A new package develops at 0.0.0.9000 and targets 0.1.0 for its first CRAN release. Set Version: 0.1.0 and the matching NEWS.md heading when the package enters Pre-flight. Bump to 0.1.0.9000 only after CRAN accepts it, never before: a .9000 version above an unreleased 0.1.0 heading is wrong.

Until the first release the R API may change freely. Sibling packages can still depend on this one before CRAN does, through Remotes: or LinkingTo:. The design (§3) names zuint, decimal and zutempo as packages that register exact types with zuarrow at load, and zuggml, zuflow, zutable, qio and quak as consumers of its stream handles. zuarrow itself waits on the zukomp release that ships the lz4 and zstd codecs (zukomp#55); that release reaches CRAN first and sets the LinkingTo floor. A package that others wait on should reach CRAN first.

Commands

Run from the package root.

Rscript -e 'devtools::load_all()'                # compile src/ and load
Rscript -e 'devtools::document()'                # roxygen -> NAMESPACE, man/
Rscript -e 'devtools::test()'                    # full testthat suite
Rscript -e 'devtools::test(filter = "<name>")'   # one test file
Rscript -e 'devtools::test(shuffle = TRUE)'      # order independence
Rscript -e 'devtools::check()'                   # R CMD check
air format .                                     # format R sources
tools/update-vendor                              # re-vendor nanoarrow, rewrite PROVENANCE
tools/verify-vendor                              # vendored tree is upstream plus patches
tools/verify-vendor --canary                     # the verifier catches a missing patch
tools/run-benchmarks [--rows N] [--reps R]       # design §10 timings, as Markdown rows
tools/bench-types [--rows N] [--reps R]          # per-type conversion against nanoarrow
NOT_CRAN=true Rscript -e 'devtools::test(filter = "abi")'   # symbol checks (skip on CRAN)

tools/fetch-fixtures                             # arrow-testing corpus into tests/testthat/fixtures
Rscript tools/make-test-data.R                   # regenerate tests/testthat/data with arrow

Oracles 1 and 2 need the arrow-testing corpus. Fetch it with tools/fetch-fixtures, or set ZUARROW_FETCH_FIXTURES=true and the tests download it under tempdir(), as CI does; without either they skip. tests/testthat/data/ holds small files written by arrow and every input the fuzz target has crashed on, so those tests run everywhere.

Architecture

Design §4 names five layers. What exists so far:

  • Vendored nanoarrow in src/vendor/nanoarrow/ (see Vendored native code).

  • Handles in src/zar_xptr.c: owning external pointers in nanoarrow’s r.h layout, readers that accept any producer’s handles, the schema copy, printing, metadata, and the spec round trip. A spec is the R list list(format, name, flags, metadata, children, dictionary) that R/handles.R builds schemas from (zar_c_schema_from_spec) and reads them back into (zar_c_schema_to_spec).

  • Validation and comparison in src/zar_validate.c, plus a strict UTF-8 pass in src/zar_utf8.c, which nanoarrow’s full level lacks.

  • Internal constructors in src/zar_build.c: arrays from raw buffers, built without validation so tests can make malformed arrays, and a stream over arrays. Tests reach them through helper-arrays.R.

  • Conversion in src/zar_to_r.c (Arrow to R) and src/zar_from_r.c (R to Arrow). zar_c_to_r takes every batch at once: a plan per column picks the R form from the type and the lossy policy, a value scan settles the columns whose exactness depends on their values (int64 past 2^53, int32 INT_MIN, a NUL in a string), and each column is then allocated once and filled from every batch. R/convert.R builds the data frame and raises the lossy conditions, naming the family package from zar_exact_target().

  • Nested conversion. A plan is a tree that mirrors the schema. A zar_slice reads a node’s elements in one batch, either directly or through a map (a dictionary’s indices, a run-end encoding’s runs), and up points at the enclosing struct, whose null rows make its fields NA. Factors take the union of every batch’s dictionary through a small hash table. Export takes list columns flattened by zar_prepare() in R, so C never calls R.

  • The registry lives in R/registry.R. Registered columns are converted in R: C leaves them (to code 9), zar_c_array_child() lends each batch’s field to the handler, and the pieces are combined with c(). A from handler’s array is moved into its slot only after the rest is finished, because nanoarrow’s finishing walks every child’s private_data as its own.

  • The IPC reader in src/zar_ipc_read.c holds the input in memory and walks the stream’s messages or the file’s footer blocks over nanoarrow’s decoder. Before decoding it verifies each header, checks every field node, buffer range, buffer alignment and compression prefix against arrow_limits() (zar_check_record_batch()), and copies a misaligned pre-0.15 message to aligned memory. Its core compiles without R under ZAR_STANDALONE for tools/fuzz/harness.c; src/zar_codecs.c is the zukomp adapter (a stub when standalone).

  • The IPC writer in src/zar_ipc_write.c encodes through ArrowIpcEncoderEncodeBatch(), which vendored patch 0013 adds: a record batch or a dictionary batch whose buffers go through zuarrow’s callback, 8-byte padded with zeros and compressed through zukomp. It writes the schema, each dictionary before the batch that first uses it, the batches, the end-of-stream marker, and for files the footer. test-write.R holds the MD5 of a fixed input in each format and codec, so a platform whose bytes differ fails.

  • Deferred strings in src/zar_altrep.c: with copy = FALSE, zar_build() turns a plain string or large_string column into an ALTREP STRSXP after the same per-value checks the copying fill makes. It keeps the batch handles in data1, caches each CHARSXP in data2 on first access, and drops the handles once every element exists. It has no serialization method, so saveRDS() writes a plain vector.

C never raises a condition. An entry point that fails frees what it owns and returns a zar_failure, list(kind, message). The R caller wraps every .Call() in zar_check(), which raises zuarrow_<kind>_error. Write the .Call() literally at the call site: R CMD check cannot see the registered routine through a variable.

Invariants that are easy to break

The design fixes these before any code exists; each has a consequence a test or CI leg will catch late. Add more as stages establish them.

  • zukomp is the only Imports (D2, D5). nanoarrow and arrow stay in Suggests; bit64 and vctrs are never imported. Adding a dependency is a design change through the RFC, not a DESCRIPTION edit.
  • Handles use nanoarrow’s r.h layout (D6): malloc()ed struct, NULL release means unset, an array’s tag holds its schema, the protected field holds what keeps the memory alive. Deviating breaks interchange with DuckDB, Polars, ADBC, arrow and nanoarrow objects.
  • Class vectors are c("zuarrow_<kind>", "nanoarrow_<kind>") and S3 methods are defined on the first class only (D7). A method on the nanoarrow_* class overwrites nanoarrow’s when both packages are loaded.
  • lossy = "error" is the default everywhere, including the as.data.frame() and as.vector() S3 methods (D4, §15 Q4). A registration may make a lossy default exact and never an exact default lossy (§6.10).
  • Vendored nanoarrow builds with NANOARROW_NAMESPACE set to zuarrow and hidden visibility, so the shared object exports R_init_zuarrow only and no Arrow* symbol (§7, §9). Without it, loading nanoarrow in the same session clashes.
  • Conversion kernels never call back into R (§4). A column that needs a registered handler is left for the R-level dispatch; a kernel that calls R can longjmp over heap it owns.
  • Validate before allocating (§6.7): nothing goes on the R heap for an IPC message that fails validation, and every IPC input gets nanoarrow’s full level. The arrow-testing crash corpus is the regression set.
  • Little-endian only in v0.1.0 (D13): a big-endian schema is a zuarrow_format_error, not a silent misread.

Testing conventions

  • Self-sufficient. Every test builds its own inputs inside the test_that() block. No file-scope objects.
  • Self-contained. Global state goes through withr::local_*(), randomised input through withr::local_seed(). Tests write only under tempdir().
  • Assert on condition classes, never message text. Use expect_error(..., class = "<pkg>_<kind>_error"). Wording belongs in snapshot tests.
  • Order independence. devtools::test(shuffle = TRUE) is part of the definition of done.
  • Borrow a conformance suite before writing one. Mainstream implementations in Python, Java, Go or Node usually ship a test corpus. Use it as an oracle rather than inventing cases by hand. None wired yet. The design (§9) names four oracles: apache/arrow-testing‘s IPC golden files and crash corpus, fetched at a pinned commit into tests/testthat/fixtures/, plus nanoarrow and arrow for interchange. The golden files do not cover big-endian reading or the codecs’ own correctness.
  • Helpers live in tests/testthat/helper-*.R. None yet.
  • Keep the suite inside the CRAN time budget. No runtime recorded yet.

Definition of done

devtools::document() and devtools::check() clean, meaning 0 errors, 0 warnings and 0 notes. The one allowed note is “New submission” before the first release. devtools::test(shuffle = TRUE) green. CI green at the change’s tier: the quick profile for a quick roadmap stage or an ordinary pull request, the full profile for a full stage, Full CI, and every release. A user-facing change also needs a test, roxygen documentation and a NEWS.md entry.

Releasing to CRAN

  • CI is the pre-submission check. The pedrobtz/r-actions R CMD check runs --as-cran on the CRAN-like runners and containers, and it replaces win-builder, the macOS builder and R-hub. None of them is a release step, and cran-comments.md lists the CI legs as its test environments.
  • Entering Pre-flight. The roadmap’s feature stages are done, the version is set as in Versioning, NEWS.md and cran-comments.md are written, and CI is green. Only submission work remains.
  • Before submitting, run pkg-critical-review once the roadmap is implemented and fix what it files, then pkg-cran-review, and resolve every finding. Both skills are in pedrobtz/r-skills.
  • The pretest is automated and does not read cran-comments.md. A NOTE that is explained but not fixed gets the upload archived. Fix the NOTE, as under Vendored native code, instead of justifying it.
  • After acceptance, pkg-post-cran tags the submitted commit with the bare version, 0.1.0 (no v), publishes the GitHub release, bumps to 0.1.0.9000, closes the version’s parent issue and moves the board card.

Editing rules

  • roxygen comments are the source. Never edit man/ or NAMESPACE by hand.
  • Edit README.Rmd, not the generated README.md.
  • Keep prose simple and short. One idea per sentence.
  • Wrap roxygen text at 80 characters and run air format . on R sources.
  • Use lower_snake_case, and prefix internal native symbols with zar_ (ZAR_ for macros), the prefix the design fixes in §3.
  • Keep hard runtime dependencies at zero unless a recorded design decision says otherwise. Here D2 records zukomp.
  • Export and document public functions. Do not create roxygen topics for internal ones.

Continuous integration

Workflows come from pedrobtz/r-actions. Call those reusable workflows instead of writing bespoke ones, and pin a released tag rather than main. Pin a workflow that holds a write token, such as coverage.yml, to a commit, with the tag in a comment. The R-CMD-check workflow must call r-cmd-check.yml, because a hand-rolled one does not count as the pre-submission check. This package calls r-cmd-check.yml@v1 from .github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml and coverage.yml@v1 from .github/workflows/coverage.yaml; .github/workflows/pkgdown.yaml is the r-lib/actions pkgdown workflow.

Small edits get a small run. The shared workflows look at the files a pull request changes, compared with its merge base:

  • Markdown only, such as README.md, NEWS.md or cran-comments.md, skips every check. Only coverage and the pkgdown site run.
  • DESCRIPTION or README.Rmd as well, and nothing else, adds one R CMD check on Ubuntu R-release.
  • Any other file runs everything.

So put a README or DESCRIPTION touch-up in its own pull request. Once a pull request changes code, every later push to it runs every workflow.

Quick by default, full by exception

The full profile is slow. gctorture at step 20 alone has taken 36 to 107 minutes on sibling packages. Waiting on it between roadmap stages was the main thing slowing roadmaps down, so:

  • Pull requests run the quick profile. It should finish in under five minutes. If it doesn’t, raise gctorture’s quick-step or trim quick-containers in the caller workflows; never cut the full profile.
  • A full roadmap stage takes the full-ci label and merges only on a green full run. The roadmap gives the reason in the stage’s **CI.** line, for example first compiled code, a PROTECT or finalizer change, a vendored library, or a Windows-only path.
  • Don’t wait on the full run a merge starts on the default branch, and cancel older full runs it supersedes. A failure that only the full set shows goes on the Full CI stage issue as a comment with the run link, and is fixed there. A failure the quick profile also shows is fixed now.
  • Full CI and v0.1.0 readiness wait for a green full run on their merge commit, and the release commit always needs one.
  • Locally, run gctorture(TRUE) on the code a C change touches when it is cheap; the full run is the authority.

Vendored native code

The nanoarrow C library’s core and ipc components, Apache-2.0, release apache-arrow-nanoarrow-0.9.0 (commit 9fad802), live under src/vendor/nanoarrow/ (design §7, D1), with the flatcc runtime nanoarrow bundles. src/vendor/PROVENANCE holds the tag, commit, archive SHA-512, the SHA-256 of every file and the patch list; inst/COPYRIGHTS and LICENSE.note carry the notices, including three MIT and one BSD flatcc header. Its integration-testing header goes into the test harness only, never into zuarrow.so (D18). lz4 and zstd are not vendored; they come from zukomp (D2).

  • The tree is derived, never edited. tools/derive-vendor downloads the release, checks the SHA-512 Apache publishes, runs upstream’s ci/scripts/bundle.py --symbol-namespace=zuarrow --with-ipc --with-flatcc, splits the generated FlatBuffers code into nanoarrow_ipc_flatcc_generated.h and applies tools/patches/ in order. tools/update-vendor writes the tree and PROVENANCE; tools/verify-vendor re-derives and fails on any byte of difference, and --canary proves it would catch a missing patch.

  • Patches. 0001-no-suppressing-pragmas removes flatcc’s #pragma diagnostic ignored lines (a NOTE); 0002-unused-locals fixes the two generated macros whose unused locals -Wall then reports (R CMD check counts “warning: unused” as significant). Every patched file carries a “Modified for the zuarrow R package” notice.

  • Visibility. src/Makevars defines NANOARROW_DLL empty, because nanoarrow otherwise marks its API visibility("default") and hidden visibility would not hide it. src/zuarrow-win.def exports R_init_zuarrow alone on Windows. test-abi.R checks both, and that nothing CRAN’s compiled-code check reports is referenced.

  • Pin a stable upstream release, never master or a release candidate.

  • Record the tag, the commit and the checksums, and write down the update procedure so the next bump is mechanical.

  • Keep upstream LICENSE and NOTICE under src/vendor/<lib>/, declare the vendored code in DESCRIPTION and inst/COPYRIGHTS.

  • Keep the vendor tree clearly separated from first-party source, and record every local patch and why it exists.

  • CRAN’s compiled-code check applies to vendored code too. No stdout or stderr, no printf, abort, exit or system RNG may be linked, even behind a debug switch that never runs. Remove them with a patch in tools/patches/, list it in src/vendor/PROVENANCE, and make the vendor-verify script check “upstream plus exactly these patches”. Avoid diagnostic-suppressing pragmas too, because they draw their own NOTE. zuhtml is the reference: tools/patches/0002-no-stdio.patch and tools/verify-vendor. zuxml’s first upload was archived because it justified such a symbol instead of patching it.

  • Guard against regressions in CI: run nm -u on the built objects and fail on any of those symbols, so an upstream bump cannot bring them back.

Commits and pull requests

Short, imperative, sentence-case commit subjects, optionally scoped. Keep each commit focused and do not sweep in unrelated files. A pull request explains the user-visible outcome and the rationale, links related issues, lists the checks that were run and the tests that were skipped, and flags platform-sensitive or vendored changes. Performance claims need evidence.

Never commit or push to the default branch. Work on a branch, open a pull request, and leave it for review. Do not merge a pull request unless you are told to.

When you find a defect, in this package or in an upstream tool, open an issue for it rather than only working around it.

Working with skills

The portfolio’s workflow skills live in pedrobtz/r-skills (pkg-init, pkg-roadmap, pkg-implement, pkg-critical-review, pkg-cran-review, pkg-post-cran, pkg-readme); the general process skills are Superpowers. building-a-package.md in pedrobtz/packages walks through them in order. Both sets defer to this file where they overlap, so the settlements are recorded here.

  • One design. The specification is .agents/design.md, adopted from the package’s RFC in pedrobtz/packages/rfcs. A package with an adopted design is past brainstorming; a design change goes through the RFC, not a new spec. Superpowers’ default docs/superpowers/specs/ is not used.
  • Plans at two levels. .agents/roadmap.md holds the stages, one mergeable pull request each, with exit criteria and a CI tier (pkg-roadmap). Inside a stage, writing-plans breaks the work into tasks of one test cycle each, saved as .agents/plans/stage-<n>.md. The roadmap stays authoritative; a plan is scratch and is not kept in sync.
  • Build and merge. pkg-implement runs the stage loop: branch stage-<n>-<slug> from the stage issue, implement the plan with test-driven-development (Rscript -e 'devtools::test(filter = "<name>")' is the red/green command), open the pull request, merge on green at the stage’s CI tier. The confirmation the user gives at the start of that loop is the “told to merge” that Commits and pull requests requires, so the finishing-a-development-branch menu is not presented for stage pull requests. Any other pull request still waits for review.
  • Failures and claims. A failing check or test goes through systematic-debugging before a fix. “Green”, “done” and “ready for CRAN” are claimed only after verification-before-completion: run the command, read the output.
  • Review. requesting-code-review gates tasks inside a stage. pkg-critical-review reviews the whole package once the roadmap is implemented, with Posit’s reviewers, and files issues. CRAN’s reviewer email and GitHub review threads go through receiving-code-review.
  • Keep scratch out of the tarball. R CMD build reads .Rbuildignore, not .gitignore. It must list ^\.agents$, ^\.superpowers$ (the Superpowers task ledger), ^\.worktrees$ (if git worktrees are kept in the package directory; a sibling directory avoids the question), ^\.claude$, ^CLAUDE\.md$, ^AGENTS\.md$, ^CRAN-SUBMISSION$ and ^cran-comments\.md$. A stray top-level file is a NOTE, and the pretest archives on NOTEs.
